content: Ownership is Rust’s most unique feature and has deep implications for the rest of the language. It enables Rust to make memory safety guarantees without needing a garbage collector, so it’s important to understand how ownership works. In this chapter, we’ll talk about ownership as well as several related features: borrowing, slices, and how Rust lays data out in memory.

content: The concepts of ownership, borrowing, and slices ensure memory safety in Rust programs at compile time. The Rust language gives you control over your memory usage in the same way as other systems programming languages. But having the owner of data automatically clean up that data when the owner goes out of scope means you don’t have to write and debug extra code to get this control.

content:
In Rust, the compiler enforces ownership
  rules through three main concepts: ownership, borrowing, and
  lifetimes.These rules ensure that for any piece of data, there
  can either be multiple immutable references or a single mutable
  reference, but not both.This principle, known as borrowing,
  significantly reduces the chances of race conditions.

content:
Slices are inherently safe because Rust’s
  borrow checker ensures that the slice does not outlive the data
  it points to, thus preventing dangling slices.Furthermore, since
  slices are a form of borrowing, they adhere to the same borrowing
  rules that apply to references.This ensures that slices respect
  the ownership and borrowing principles that Rust enforces for
  memory safety.

content: Rust’s borrow checker can’t understand that we’re borrowing different parts of the slice; it only knows that we’re borrowing from the same slice twice. Borrowing different parts of a slice is fundamentally okay because the two slices aren’t overlapping, but Rust isn’t smart enough to know this. When we know code is okay, but Rust doesn’t, it’s time to reach for unsafe code.

​Ownership and BorrowingAt the heart of
  Rust’s performance lies its ownership model, complemented by the
  rules of borrowing.These features ensure memory safety without
  the overhead of a garbage collector.When a variable goes out of
  scope, Rust automatically calls thedropfunction to free its resources,
  preventing memory leaks.This design decision eliminates the need
  for a runtime-enforced garbage collection, reducing overhead and
  leading to more predictable performance.

content: Rust’s ownership rules have saved us again! We got an error from the code inListing 16-3because Rust was being conservative and only borrowingvfor the thread, which meant the main thread could theoretically invalidate the spawned thread’s reference. By telling Rust to move ownership ofvto the spawned thread, we’re guaranteeing to Rust that the main thread won’t usevanymore. If we changeListing 16-4in the same way, we’re then violating the ownership rules when we try to usevin the main thread. Themovekeyword overrides Rust’s conservative default of borrowing; it doesn’t let us violate the ownership rules.

content:
A slice in Rust is a two-word object, the
  first word is a pointer to the data, and the second word is the
  length of the slice.This means that a slice lets you reference a
  contiguous sequence of elements in a collection rather than the
  whole collection.For example, a slice can refer to a part of an
  array or a subsection of a String.This feature is particularly
  useful for passing parts of data structures to functions without
  transferring ownership.

  alternative to references for working with parts of collections.They inherit the safety and efficiency of Rust’s borrowing
  system, allowing programmers to write more flexible and
  performant code.Understanding and using slices effectively is a
  key skill in Rust programming, especially for operations on
  sequences of data.​
